Along the way, we stopped in Fatima, a peaceful town in central Portugal known for its famous Catholic pilgrimage site, the Sanctuary of our Lady Fatima. 

The reason millions come here each year, is related to an event which took place in the early 20th century. This event involved three local children, Lúcia dos Santos and her cousins, Francisco and Jacinta Marto, who saw visions of a woman known as Our Lady of Fátima, since believed by the Catholic Church to be the Virgin Mary. On 13 May 1917, while guarding their families' sheep in the Cova da Iria, the children first claimed to have seen an apparition of a "lady dressed in white" and shining with a bright light.

Because of this, The city of Fatima has become an important international destination for religious tourists, receiving between 6 and 8 million pilgrims yearly.

Today, we were there to see thousands of people observing Mass outside of the Basilica. 

On the same site, a statue of Pope John Paul II, who was very popular in Portugal, and a piece of the Berlin Wall.

After leaving Fatima, we spent time in a quaint historic village town called Óbidos. It’s well preserved, and is a perfect place to grab a bite to eat, or shop for souvenirs. 

We then landed in Lisbon, with a city tour and more shopping on tap for Day 10 (Monday, April 20th)

Along the way, we stopped in Fatima, a peaceful town in central Portugal known for its famous Catholic pilgrimage site, the Sanctuary of our Lady Fatima. 

The reason millions come here each year, is related to an event which took place in the early 20th century. This event involved three local children, Lúcia dos Santos and her cousins, Francisco and Jacinta Marto, who saw visions of a woman known as Our Lady of Fátima, since believed by the Catholic Church to be the Virgin Mary. On 13 May 1917, while guarding their families' sheep in the Cova da Iria, the children first claimed to have seen an apparition of a "lady dressed in white" and shining with a bright light.

Because of this, The city of Fatima has become an important international destination for religious tourists, receiving between 6 and 8 million pilgrims yearly.

Today, we were there to see thousands of people observing Mass outside of the Basilica. 

On the same site, a statue of Pope John Paul II, who was very popular in Portugal, and a piece of the Berlin Wall.

After leaving Fatima, we spent time in a quaint historic village town called Óbidos. It’s well preserved, and is a perfect place to grab a bite to eat, or shop for souvenirs. 

We then landed in Lisbon, with a city tour and more shopping on tap for Day 10 (Monday, April 20th)

# Henry the Navigator Leads Order of Christ

Henry the Navigator, a key figure in the Age of Exploration, was awarded the governorship of the Order of Christ on May 25, 1420. This powerful religious order, associated with the Knights Templar, provided him with the financial resources necessary to pursue his ambitious goals in navigation and exploration. Born in 1394, Henry was the third son of King John I of Portugal and sought alternative avenues for influence rather than the throne. His military interests began with the conquest of the Muslim port city of Ceuta in 1415, which sparked his fascination with trade routes.

Henry established a center for navigation in Sagres, Portugal, where he developed new technologies and methods for sea exploration. He founded a school for navigators, created an observatory, and promoted innovations in ship design, notably the caravel. While he never personally embarked on voyages, his initiatives led to significant discoveries, including the Madeira Islands and the Azores, and advancements along the African coast. His efforts, supported by the profits of the Order of Christ, ultimately laid the groundwork for Portugal's expansive trade empire across the globe, significantly impacting the region's economic dynamics. Henry passed away in 1460, but his legacy continued to influence maritime exploration and trade for generations.

### Henry the Navigator Leads Order of Christ

On May 25, 1420, Prince Henry of Portugal, nicknamed the Navigator, was awarded the governorship of the Order of Christ, the Portuguese branch of one of the world's wealthiest religious orders, the Knights Templar. The revenue from this post would help Henry pursue his interests in navigation and exploration and make him a pioneer in Europe's nascent colonial expansion. He was one of the founders of Portugal's trade empire, which at its peak stretched from Brazil to Africa to the East Indies.

Henry was born sometime in 1394 in Porto, Portugal. He was the third son of the Portuguese king John I and thus unlikely ever to succeed to the throne. Therefore, he pursued other interests. Henry encouraged his father to cross the straits of Gibraltar and attack the Muslim port city of Ceuta in North Africa, not far from Portugal and he conquered it in 1415. Henry was impressed with the city's prosperity, based on trade, and became convinced that Portugal should pursue trading possibilities as well. However, rather than deal with the Muslim middlemen who dominated Asian and African trade with Europe, Henry wanted to develop Portugal's own trade routes. He moved to Sagres in southern Portugal, close to North Africa, and began to establish institutions for the expansion of Portuguese sea power, which would be essential in building his visionary trade empire. The Portuguese already had a long seafaring tradition, but Henry's new school for navigators expanded upon these skills and made the latest scientific information available. He also established an observatory, so that navigators using the stars and other heavenly bodies for guidance would have precise information. Finally, Henry encouraged improvements in ship design and construction, which led to the development of a new kind of sailing vessel, known as the caravel.

Although he never went on a single voyage himself, Henry's navigators and explorers discovered the Madeira Islands and the Azores in the Atlantic Ocean, both of which were colonized by the Portuguese. His seamen also sailed south along the African coastline, and in 1434 they passed Cape Bojador, the southernmost point known to any European sailor. Terrifying old stories warned of a “green sea of darkness” swarming with monsters beyond Cape Bojador, but the Portuguese rounded the cape and discovered that there were no monsters there. Much encouraged, Henry pushed his men to explore farther, in voyages made possible by the revenue from his position as head of the Order of Christ. The Portuguese Crown also granted him one-fifth of any profits that might be derived from new trade beyond Bojador. By 1446 Henry's men had reached the mouth of the Gambia River in equatorial Africa, charting many sites as they traveled that would later become Portuguese trading posts and forts. Even before he died on November 13, 1460, the fruits of Henry's labors were being realized, as gold and other riches flowed directly into Portuguese coffers, now that the Muslim traders using land routes across mainland Africa could be bypassed.

Henry the Navigator, a key figure in the Age of Exploration, was awarded the governorship of the Order of Christ on May 25, 1420. This powerful religious order, associated with the Knights Templar, provided him with the financial resources necessary to pursue his ambitious goals in navigation and exploration. His military interests began with the conquest of the Muslim port city of Ceuta in 1415, which sparked his fascination with trade routes.

Henry established a center for navigation in Sagres, Portugal, where he developed new technologies and methods for sea exploration. He founded a school for navigators, created an observatory, and promoted innovations in ship design, notably the caravel. While he never personally embarked on voyages, his initiatives led to significant discoveries, including the Madeira Islands and the Azores, and advancements along the African coast. His efforts, supported by the profits of the Order of Christ, ultimately laid the groundwork for Portugal's expansive trade empire across the globe, significantly impacting the region's economic dynamics. Henry passed away in 1460, but his legacy continued to influence maritime exploration and trade for generations.

### Henry the Navigator Leads Order of Christ

On May 25, 1420, Prince Henry of Portugal, nicknamed the Navigator, was awarded the governorship of the Order of Christ, the Portuguese branch of one of the world's wealthiest religious orders, the Knights Templar. The revenue from this post would help Henry pursue his interests in navigation and exploration and make him a pioneer in Europe's nascent colonial expansion. He was one of the founders of Portugal's trade empire, which at its peak stretched from Brazil to Africa to the East Indies.

Henry was born sometime in 1394 in Porto, Portugal. He was the third son of the Portuguese king John I and thus unlikely ever to succeed to the throne. Therefore, he pursued other interests. Henry encouraged his father to cross the straits of Gibraltar and attack the Muslim port city of Ceuta in North Africa, not far from Portugal and he conquered it in 1415. Henry was impressed with the city's prosperity, based on trade, and became convinced that Portugal should pursue trading possibilities as well. However, rather than deal with the Muslim middlemen who dominated Asian and African trade with Europe, Henry wanted to develop Portugal's own trade routes. He moved to Sagres in southern Portugal, close to North Africa, and began to establish institutions for the expansion of Portuguese sea power, which would be essential in building his visionary trade empire. The Portuguese already had a long seafaring tradition, but Henry's new school for navigators expanded upon these skills and made the latest scientific information available. He also established an observatory, so that navigators using the stars and other heavenly bodies for guidance would have precise information. Finally, Henry encouraged improvements in ship design and construction, which led to the development of a new kind of sailing vessel, known as the caravel.

Although he never went on a single voyage himself, Henry's navigators and explorers discovered the Madeira Islands and the Azores in the Atlantic Ocean, both of which were colonized by the Portuguese. His seamen also sailed south along the African coastline, and in 1434 they passed Cape Bojador, the southernmost point known to any European sailor. Terrifying old stories warned of a “green sea of darkness” swarming with monsters beyond Cape Bojador, but the Portuguese rounded the cape and discovered that there were no monsters there. Much encouraged, Henry pushed his men to explore farther, in voyages made possible by the revenue from his position as head of the Order of Christ. The Portuguese Crown also granted him one-fifth of any profits that might be derived from new trade beyond Bojador. By 1446 Henry's men had reached the mouth of the Gambia River in equatorial Africa, charting many sites as they traveled that would later become Portuguese trading posts and forts. Even before he died on November 13, 1460, the fruits of Henry's labors were being realized, as gold and other riches flowed directly into Portuguese coffers, now that the Muslim traders using land routes across mainland Africa could be bypassed.

# Vasco da Gama

## Explorer

### Age of Discovery

**Quick Facts:**

Portuguese explorer and navigator who found a direct sea route from Europe to Asia, and was the first European to sail to India by going around Africa.

**Name**: Vasco da Gama [vas-koh]; [(Portuguese) vahsh-koo] [duh gah-muh]

**Birth/Death**: ca. 1460 CE - 1524 CE

**Nationality**: Portuguese

**Birthplace**: Portugal

[![Image 2: Vasco da Gama portrait](https://exploration.marinersmuseum.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2014/02/Vasco-da-Gama.png)](https://exploration.marinersmuseum.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2014/02/Vasco-da-Gama.png "Vasco da Gama")[](https://exploration.marinersmuseum.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2014/02/Vasco-da-Gama.png "Vasco da Gama")
## Vasco da Gama

Portrait of Vasco da Gama by artist Antonio Manuel da Fonseca in 1838. Vasco da Gama, (c.1469 – 1524) was a Portuguese explorer, one of the most successful in the European Age of Discovery and the commander of the first ships to sail directly from Europe to India. (Credit: National Maritime Museum)

Introduction  
 Vasco da Gama was a Portuguese explorer who sailed to India from Europe. Gold, spices, and other riches were valuable in Europe. But they had to navigate long ways over sea and land to reach them in Asia. Europeans during this time were looking to find a faster way to reach India by sailing around Africa. Da Gama accomplished the task. By doing so, he helped open a major trade route to Asia. Portugal celebrated his success, and his voyage launched a new era of discovery and world trade.

Biography  
 Early Life  
Vasco da Gama’s exact birthdate and place is unknown. It is believed he was born between 1460 and 1469 in Sines, Portugal.1 He was the third son to his parents. His father, Estêvão da Gama, was a knight in the Duke of Viseu’s court; and his mother was a noblewoman named Isabel Sodré.2 His father’s role in the court would have allowed young Vasco to have a good education. But because he lived close to a seaport town, he probably also learned about ships and navigation. Vasco attended school in a larger village about 70 miles from Sines called Évora. Here, he learned advanced mathematics, and studied principles of navigation. By fifteen he became familiar with trading ships that were docked in port. By the age of twenty, he was the captain of a ship.3 These skills would all make him an acceptable choice to lead an expedition to India.

Vasco da Gama’s maritime career was during the period when Portugal was searching for a trade route around Africa to India. The Ottoman Empire controlled almost all European trade routes to Asia. This meant they could, and did, charge high prices for ships passing through ports. Prince Henry of Portugal – also called Prince Henry the Navigator – began Portugal’s great age of exploration. From about 1419 until his death in 1460, he sent several sailing expeditions down the coast of Africa.4 In 1481, King John II of Portugal began sending expeditions to find a sea route around the southern shores of Africa. Many explorers made several attempts. It was Bartolomeu Dias who was the first to round Africa and make it to the Indian Ocean in 1488. But he was forced to head back to Portugal before he could make it to India. When Manuel I became king of Portugal in 1495, he continued efforts to open a trade route to India by going around Africa. Although other people were considered for the job, Manuel I finally chose thirty-seven year old Vasco da Gama for this task.

Voyages  
Principal Voyage  
On 8 July 1497 Vasco da Gama sailed from Lisbon with a fleet of four ships with a crew of 170 men from Lisbon. Da Gama commanded the _Sao Gabriel_. Paulo da Gama – brother to Vasco – commanded the _São Rafael_, a three masted ship. There was also the caravel _Berrio_, and a storeship _São Maria_. Bartolomeu Dias also sailed with da Gama, and gave helpful advice for navigating down the African coast. They sailed past the Canary Islands, and reached the Cape Verde islands by July 26. They stayed about a week, then continued sailing on August 3. To help avoid the storms and strong currents near the Gulf of Guinea, da Gama and his fleet sailed out into the South Atlantic and swung down to the Cape of Good Hope. ## Quick Reference

Upon first look at his name, it would make sense to assume that Prince Henry the Navigator of Portugal earned his name through voyages and exploration. However, that is not the case, even though many still ascribe the term “Navigator” to Prince Henry in writings. He derived his name from the many voyages that he sponsored to the New World and beyond.

Henry was born in March of 1394 to King John I and Philippa of Lancaster in Porto, Portugal. In 1420, Henry was made the leader of a religious group in Portugal known as the Order of Christ. With much of the money that came in to support this group, Henry was able to fund explorations that took place across the Atlantic Ocean and down the West Coast of Africa. Henry was attracted by the potential riches that he could find on the African continent, specifically the amounts of gold and the enslaved people that he could acquire for Portugal in his quest to bring wealth to his country. Prince Henry also wanted to build up his number of Christian allies, improve his knowledge of geography, and find a sea route to Asia.

![Image 4: Prince Henry the Navigator](https://kajabi-storefronts-production.kajabi-cdn.com/kajabi-storefronts-production/file-uploads/themes/2153302878/settings_images/71540fa-c185-86a6-df36-8bc878cf7e0_cUTZwzjRRcyqUzLVcWJw_prince_Henry_the_Navigator.jpg)

Prince Henry is also remembered for two important contributions to the fate of Portuguese exploration. Around 1418, he opened the first school for oceanic navigation, where students could learn about map-making, scientific practices, astronomy, and more skills that would aid them in their journey down the west coast of Africa.

The second contribution was the founding of the Transatlantic slave trade. Two of his captains, Antao Goncalves and Nuno Tristao, had ventured to Cape Bianco in what is now Tunisia. The two men were the first Europeans to buy enslaved Africans and brought several of them back to Europe. It began with twelve kidnapped men and women the first year, and then many more in the following years as the slave trade grew in size, influence, and power. Prince Henry was in power and oversaw these voyages actively until his death in 1460.

## Prince Henry The Navigator

 By Winston B. Lewis 

November 1960

Proceedings

Vol. 86/11/693

Article

[View Issue](https://www.usni.org/magazines/proceedings/1960/november)

[Facebook](https://www.usni.org/#facebook)[Twitter](https://www.usni.org/#twitter)[Reddit](https://www.usni.org/#reddit)[Email](https://www.usni.org/#email)[Share](https://www.addtoany.com/share#url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.usni.org%2Fmagazines%2Fproceedings%2F1960%2Fnovember%2Fprince-henry-navigator&title=Prince%20Henry%20The%20Navigator)

Comments

Last August, ships of the U. S. Navy joined vessels from all over the world in a great naval parade off Cape St. Vincent, the Sagres of the fifteenth century. The ceremony was a most appropriate tribute on the 500th anniversary of the death of Prince Henry the Navigator, the man who, in effect, opened the seas to navigation and began the discovery of the modern world. When he came upon the scene, Europe was Medieval; its geographical knowledge was confined principally to the continent itself, a little of the Middle East, and the North African littoral; sailors regarded with superstitious terror the seas beyond the familiar coastal waters. When he died, the west coast of Africa had been explored and accurately charted to Sierra Leone; the Madeiras, the Azores, and the Cape Verde Islands had been discovered or rediscovered; and even Brazil may have been sighted and Newfoundland approached by his captains. More important, unfounded fears had vanished, and mariners could sail the seas with the confidence that they faced only natural dangers.

The person who achieved this transition from the Medieval to the Modern was a strange mixture of the characteristics of a man of both eras. He was fired all his life by a crusading fervor. He won his knighthood in taking Ceuta from the Moors, he was in his forties when he led the ill-fated crusade against Tangier, and the desire to spread the Christian faith was no small part of the motivation for his explorations. On the modern side was his desire for knowledge, “from which,” as he wrote, “all good things arise.” The search for it dominated his whole life and led him to send out expedition after expedition, “because,” explains Azurara, the principal chronicler of this phase of Portuguese history, “he desired to know what lands there were beyond the Canary Isles and a cape called Bojador, for up to that time no one knew, whether by writing or the memory of any man, what might be beyond this cape.” After mentioning the legends, Azurara continues, “And the Infante Dom Henrique desired to know the truth of this; for it seemed to him that if he or some other lord did not essay to discover this, no sailor or merchant would undertake this effort, for it is very sure that these do not think to navigate other where than to places where they already know that they will find their profit. And seeing that no other prince was concerning himself with the matter, he sent his own ships to these countries in order to acquire certitude.”

It may have been the conquest of Ceuta that started Prince Henry thinking of Africa and what lay beyond, for it was shortly after his return that he began his residence at Sagres and sent out his first expeditions. Sagres is a rocky, desolate promontory which forms the southwesternmost tip of Portugal. At first Henry resided at the little village of Raposeira, a few miles inland. Later he began his _Villa do Infante_ on the cape itself, with a chapel, warehouses, a palace, a study, and even an observatory. His choice of this spot for a base was both imaginative and practical: imaginative because the cape jutted into and was surrounded by the ocean he was determined to explore; practical because in its lee, vessels from the Mediterranean waited for a favorable wind to proceed to northern Europe. It was indeed such a useful entrepôt that, after Henry had developed it, the Genoese, whose business acumen was famous, offered to buy it for an immense sum.

There Prince Henry gathered his famous “School of Sagres.” Although it was not a school in any formal sense, it was probably the first university of practical science in Europe, for there Henry gathered a wonderfully cosmopolitan group of mathematicians, astronomers, cartographers, cosmographers, instrument makers—all who might contribute to his great purpose. Here, too, Henry gathered and trained interpreters and missionaries to accompany his expeditions, so that at Sagres one might find not only distinguished scholars or adventurous captains from any country of Europe, but also Arabs, Berbers, Azenegues from the Sahara, and apparently even Ethiopians and Indians. One can understand why Henry’s brother Pedro, who returned in 1428 from a tour of Europe, could find no more appropriate presents for his brother than a great Venetian _mappa mundi_ and a copy of Marco Polo’s travels.

At Sagres Henry planned and at Lagos Bay he equipped the expeditions which were his life’s work. The first, sent out in 1415, visited the Canaries, already known but not explored—the Canaries tempted Henry greatly, but since they were claimed by Castille, he had to keep his hands off them. Three years later an expedition to the Guinea coast was driven off course and discovered Porto Santo in the Madeiras, which Henry soon explored and undertook to colonize—the first European colony in modern history. But Henry’s first major objective was to pass Cape Bojador, on the African coast just below the Canaries, which represented not only the limit of previous exploration, but also a psychological barrier, since it was believed that beyond it the seas became unnavigable and that no ship which passed it would ever return. From 1421 onward Henry regularly sent out ships with orders to pass beyond the cape, but his captains and crews always found excuses to turn back short of their goal. Henry rewarded them for what they had accomplished, was patient in regard to what they had not—and sent them out again. When in 1433 Gil Eannes went only to the Canaries before returning, the Infante spoke to him seriously:

“I want you to pass beyond Cape Bojador—if you do nothing more than pass this cape, I shall be satisfied ... You cannot meet there a peril so great that the hope of reward shall not be even greater. In truth, I marvel at these imaginings which have possessed you all, and of matters so uncertain. If these things possessed any authority, even though that authority were small, I might still find excuse for you; but I am astonished to think that you have them from the opinion of some few mariners who know only the navigation of Flanders and other ports to which they are accustomed to resort, and do not know how to handle a compass or make use of a chart of the seas. Have, therefore, no fear of their opinion in undertaking your voyage, because, with the grace of God, you shall derive therefrom only honour and profit.”

Thus admonished, Gil Eannes this time did pass beyond Cape Bojador, finding, rather to his surprise it seems, “the seas as easy to sail in as the waters at home.” He landed in a boat and found only a sandy shore with sparse vegetation, some samples of which he took back to his master in 1434. Prince Henry was doubtless more pleased with these dried plants than with any of the Moorish treasure with which his other captains had returned.

After this “breakthrough” there was no longer any difficulty in persuading his captains to pass the cape, and by 1436 they had reached the Rio de Ouro. But the promise of rapid progress was short-lived, for from 1436 to 1441 the expeditions had to be suspended. The reason was the distraction of other affairs: Henry’s leadership of the disastrous Tangier crusade in 1437, the death of his brother, King Edward, and the disorders attending the minority of Edward’s son. Prince Henry always found politics distasteful, but he was forced for the moment to abandon his own projects to give his attention to family and national concerns.

Henry returned to Sagres and to launching expeditions in 1441. In that year Nuno Tristam reached Cape Blanco, and the following year he arrived at the Bay of Arguim, where a few years later Henry erected a fort that was to become a center of the slave trade. For when some of Henry’s captains returned with gold dust and slaves, the trading world suddenly found an interest in Henry’s activities. In 1443 a royal decree granted the Prince the sole right to send vessels south of Cape Bojador and one-fifth of all profits from the area, so that Henry, now building his town at Sagres, was besieged by merchants seeking his license for voyages to the Guinea coast.

Henry had encouraged his first expeditions to bring back a few of the natives. His purpose was clearly scientific—he wanted to learn what he could of their country, their race, their customs, their language—in short, he was beginning the science of ethnology. There was the almost equally important consideration, of course, of saving their souls by making them Christians—one of Henry’s projects was to train natives to return as missionaries to their people. But the traders, and many even of the prince’s own captains, were far more interested in the profits of the slave trade than in science or the saving of souls. This preoccupation with slaving partially explains the slow progress of exploration in the next few years, for once a captain had reached a spot at which he could gather a cargo of slaves there was little point in going further.

There was, however, some forward movement. In 1445 Diniz Diaz and Nuno Tristam reached the Senegal, and Diaz pressed on to reach Cape Verde. In 1446 Tristam, one of the few who seems genuinely to have shared Prince Henry’s purpose, passed almost two hundred miles beyond Cape Verde but, while exploring a river in small boats, he and his men were ambushed by natives shooting poisoned arrows, so that only five survived to sail their ship home. In the same year Alvaro Fernandez, with orders to go as far as he could, pushed on—despite a poisoned arrow wound incurred at a landing on the way—to a point 320 miles beyond the cape or approximately to the modern Sierra Leone. This was the farthest point reached during Henry’s lifetime. While many ships sailed during the next few years, their captains were content to pick up a cargo of slaves and return.

The probing of the Atlantic, the discovery of the Azores, and the addition of twelve or thirteen hundred miles to the known coast of Africa may seem small enough in comparison with the great voyages of only a few years later, but the accomplishment was tremendous in comparison with what had been done in the centuries preceding. Moreover, it represented the pioneering that swept aside superstition and proved what could be done. Diaz’s discovery of the Cape of Good Hope in 1487 and Vasco da Gama’s great voyage to the Far East in 1497-98 were direct continuations of the work begun by Prince Henry. Even Columbus had served eight or nine years with the Portuguese before his great voyage and used the Azores as a springboard.

There was another side of the accomplishment, too. The legend that no ship returned from beyond Cape Bojador was not altogether a myth, for before Henry’s time it is probable that no ship was capable of returning against the adverse winds and currents of the African coast. It was the Portuguese development of the handy, weatherly caravel that made fifteenth-century exploration feasible. It was and remained for some time the type best suited for exploration. Its development from a fishing vessel came in Prince Henry’s time and, while the details are lost, it is a good surmise that he had a hand in it. Certainly it was he who brought to bear the scientific knowledge of the day to provide the best system of navigation and the most accurate charts possible.

The man himself is too complex to be captured by any description, though Azurara gives us an excellent one:

He had force of mind and acute intelligence in a high degree. His desire to accomplish great deeds was beyond all comparison. Lust and avarice never obtained a hold upon his heart . . ., His house gave welcome to all men of the realm who possessed merit, and even more to foreigners whose renown justified the expense he was at to have them there; for as an ordinary thing he had about him men of different countries, men of very distant countries, and all held him for a great marvel, and never departed without receiving great benefits from him. All his days were filled with assiduous labour; for surely among all the nations of mankind one could not find any more able than he to subdue himself. It would be hard indeed to count the nights during which his eyes knew no sleep . . . He was quiet in manner, and his words were calm; in adversity he was constant, and humble in prosperity. Never was known in him hatred or ill-will toward any, even though heavy faults were committed against him . . .

The ceremonies in his honor began last March with a national holiday and a _Te Deum_ in all Portuguese cathedrals, followed by a pilgrimage by students of the University of Coimbra, of which Prince Henry was Protector and for which he did much, to his tomb in the Monastery of Batalha. In August occurred the great naval parade off Sagres. Commemorative stamps and coins have been issued, and a great series of historical works on Prince Henry and Portuguese exploration is being published. The ceremonies culminate on 13 November the date of Prince Henry’s death in 1460. The world joins Portugal in honoring her great Prince, who laid the foundations for the age of discovery and was among the first of our modern men of science.

An associate professor in the Department of English, History, and Government at the U. S. Naval Academy, **Mr. Lewis** was on active duty from 1941-45 in the Publication Section, ONI. He is the author of B _attle of Midway, Java Sea Campaign_, and _Savo Island_, as well as co-author of _Sicilian Campaign_, all in the ONI series. In addition he is co-author of the following books: _The United States in World Sea Power, Sea Power_, and _The Great Sea War_.

November 1960

“I want you to pass beyond Cape Bojador—if you do nothing more than pass this cape, I shall be satisfied ... You cannot meet there a peril so great that the hope of reward shall not be even greater. In truth, I marvel at these imaginings which have possessed you all, and of matters so uncertain. If these things possessed any authority, even though that authority were small, I might still find excuse for you; but I am astonished to think that you have them from the opinion of some few mariners who know only the navigation of Flanders and other ports to which they are accustomed to resort, and do not know how to handle a compass or make use of a chart of the seas. Have, therefore, no fear of their opinion in undertaking your voyage, because, with the grace of God, you shall derive therefrom only honour and profit.”

Thus admonished, Gil Eannes this time did pass beyond Cape Bojador, finding, rather to his surprise it seems, “the seas as easy to sail in as the waters at home.” He landed in a boat and found only a sandy shore with sparse vegetation, some samples of which he took back to his master in 1434. Prince Henry was doubtless more pleased with these dried plants than with any of the Moorish treasure with which his other captains had returned.

After this “breakthrough” there was no longer any difficulty in persuading his captains to pass the cape, and by 1436 they had reached the Rio de Ouro. But the promise of rapid progress was short-lived, for from 1436 to 1441 the expeditions had to be suspended. The reason was the distraction of other affairs: Henry’s leadership of the disastrous Tangier crusade in 1437, the death of his brother, King Edward, and the disorders attending the minority of Edward’s son. Prince Henry always found politics distasteful, but he was forced for the moment to abandon his own projects to give his attention to family and national concerns.

Henry returned to Sagres and to launching expeditions in 1441. In that year Nuno Tristam reached Cape Blanco, and the following year he arrived at the Bay of Arguim, where a few years later Henry erected a fort that was to become a center of the slave trade. For when some of Henry’s captains returned with gold dust and slaves, the trading world suddenly found an interest in Henry’s activities. In 1443 a royal decree granted the Prince the sole right to send vessels south of Cape Bojador and one-fifth of all profits from the area, so that Henry, now building his town at Sagres, was besieged by merchants seeking his license for voyages to the Guinea coast.

Henry had encouraged his first expeditions to bring back a few of the natives. His purpose was clearly scientific—he wanted to learn what he could of their country, their race, their customs, their language—in short, he was beginning the science of ethnology. There was the almost equally important consideration, of course, of saving their souls by making them Christians—one of Henry’s projects was to train natives to return as missionaries to their people. But the traders, and many even of the prince’s own captains, were far more interested in the profits of the slave trade than in science or the saving of souls. This preoccupation with slaving partially explains the slow progress of exploration in the next few years, for once a captain had reached a spot at which he could gather a cargo of slaves there was little point in going further.

There was, however, some forward movement. In 1445 Diniz Diaz and Nuno Tristam reached the Senegal, and Diaz pressed on to reach Cape Verde. In 1446 Tristam, one of the few who seems genuinely to have shared Prince Henry’s purpose, passed almost two hundred miles beyond Cape Verde but, while exploring a river in small boats, he and his men were ambushed by natives shooting poisoned arrows, so that only five survived to sail their ship home. In the same year Alvaro Fernandez, with orders to go as far as he could, pushed on—despite a poisoned arrow wound incurred at a landing on the way—to a point 320 miles beyond the cape or approximately to the modern Sierra Leone. This was the farthest point reached during Henry’s lifetime. While many ships sailed during the next few years, their captains were content to pick up a cargo of slaves and return.

The probing of the Atlantic, the discovery of the Azores, and the addition of twelve or thirteen hundred miles to the known coast of Africa may seem small enough in comparison with the great voyages of only a few years later, but the accomplishment was tremendous in comparison with what had been done in the centuries preceding. Moreover, it represented the pioneering that swept aside superstition and proved what could be done. Diaz’s discovery of the Cape of Good Hope in 1487 and Vasco da Gama’s great voyage to the Far East in 1497-98 were direct continuations of the work begun by Prince Henry. Even Columbus had served eight or nine years with the Portuguese before his great voyage and used the Azores as a springboard.

There was another side of the accomplishment, too. The legend that no ship returned from beyond Cape Bojador was not altogether a myth, for before Henry’s time it is probable that no ship was capable of returning against the adverse winds and currents of the African coast. It was the Portuguese development of the handy, weatherly caravel that made fifteenth-century exploration feasible. It was and remained for some time the type best suited for exploration. Its development from a fishing vessel came in Prince Henry’s time and, while the details are lost, it is a good surmise that he had a hand in it. Certainly it was he who brought to bear the scientific knowledge of the day to provide the best system of navigation and the most accurate charts possible.

The man himself is too complex to be captured by any description, though Azurara gives us an excellent one:

He had force of mind and acute intelligence in a high degree. His desire to accomplish great deeds was beyond all comparison. Lust and avarice never obtained a hold upon his heart . . ., His house gave welcome to all men of the realm who possessed merit, and even more to foreigners whose renown justified the expense he was at to have them there; for as an ordinary thing he had about him men of different countries, men of very distant countries, and all held him for a great marvel, and never departed without receiving great benefits from him. All his days were filled with assiduous labour; for surely among all the nations of mankind one could not find any more able than he to subdue himself. It would be hard indeed to count the nights during which his eyes knew no sleep . . . He was quiet in manner, and his words were calm; in adversity he was constant, and humble in prosperity. Never was known in him hatred or ill-will toward any, even though heavy faults were committed against him . . .

The ceremonies in his honor began last March with a national holiday and a _Te Deum_ in all Portuguese cathedrals, followed by a pilgrimage by students of the University of Coimbra, of which Prince Henry was Protector and for which he did much, to his tomb in the Monastery of Batalha. In August occurred the great naval parade off Sagres. Commemorative stamps and coins have been issued, and a great series of historical works on Prince Henry and Portuguese exploration is being published. The ceremonies culminate on 13 November the date of Prince Henry’s death in 1460. The world joins Portugal in honoring her great Prince, who laid the foundations for the age of discovery and was among the first of our modern men of science.

An associate professor in the Department of English, History, and Government at the U. S. Naval Academy, **Mr. Lewis** was on active duty from 1941-45 in the Publication Section, ONI. **Prince Henry the Navigator**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-1) (4 March 1394 – 13 December 1460), was a [Portuguese prince](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infante_of_Portugal "Infante of Portugal"), a central figure in the early days of the [Portuguese Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Empire "Portuguese Empire") and often credited as one of the main initiators of the [Age of Discovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Discovery "Age of Discovery"). Henry was the third child of King [John I of Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_I_of_Portugal "John I of Portugal"), who founded the [House of Aviz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Aviz "House of Aviz").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-2)

Utilising the new [caravel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caravel "Caravel") ship, Henry directed the early development of Portuguese exploration and maritime trade with other continents through the systematic exploration of Western Africa, the islands of the Atlantic Ocean, and the search for new routes. He supported his father in the 1415 [conquest of Ceuta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_conquest_of_Ceuta "Portuguese conquest of Ceuta"), a Muslim port on the North African coast across the [Straits of Gibraltar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straits_of_Gibraltar "Straits of Gibraltar") from the [Iberian Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberian_Peninsula "Iberian Peninsula"). Regarded as the patron of [Portuguese discoveries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_discoveries "Portuguese discoveries"), he died on 13 November 1460 in Vila do Bispo in the [Algarve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algarve "Algarve").

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Prince_Henry_the_Navigator&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/21/Casa_do_Infante_%28Porto%29.JPG/250px-Casa_do_Infante_%28Porto%29.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Casa_do_Infante_(Porto).JPG)

The [Casa do Infante](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casa_do_Infante "Casa do Infante"), in [Porto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porto "Porto"), is traditionally considered Prince Henry's birthplace.

Henry was the third surviving son of [King John I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_I_of_Portugal "John I of Portugal") and his wife [Philippa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippa_of_Lancaster "Philippa of Lancaster"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-mariners-3) sister of [King Henry IV of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_IV_of_England "Henry IV of England"). He was baptized in [Porto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porto "Porto"), and may have been born there, probably when the royal couple was living in the city's old mint, now called [Casa do Infante](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casa_do_Infante "Casa do Infante") (Prince's House), or in the region nearby. Another possibility is that he was born at the Monastery of Leça do Balio, in [Leça da Palmeira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_of_Le%C3%A7a_da_Palmeira "Fort of Leça da Palmeira"), during the same period of the royal couple's residence in the city of Porto.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-Bradford,_1960-4)

As early as 1410 or 1412, Henry had commissioned his captains to explore the coasts beyond [Cape Non](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Chaunar "Cape Chaunar"), which was considered the limit of the known and charted world in Europe together with [Cape Bojador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Bojador "Cape Bojador").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:0-5) Little is known of these expeditions, however.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:0-5)

### The conquest of Ceuta, 1415

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Prince_Henry_the_Navigator&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: The conquest of Ceuta, 1415")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bc/Africa_Portuguese_Empire_1342-1801.png/250px-Africa_Portuguese_Empire_1342-1801.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Africa_Portuguese_Empire_1342-1801.png)

Portuguese presence and exploration in Africa and middle east -1415 - 1801

Henry was 21 when he participated in [an expedition to capture the Moorish port city of Ceuta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conquest_of_Ceuta "Conquest of Ceuta") in northern [Morocco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morocco "Morocco"). Henry was made responsible for recruiting troops and ships in northern Portugal and assemble them at Porto before joining the main fleet en route to Ceuta. At Ceuta, he anchored his ships off the lower part of the town, and on the 15th of August king John rowed through the fleet to inspect it as the attack was to take place the following morning.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:12-6) Henry was said to have claimed and been granted the right to be the first to land. The quays were expected to be devoid of defenders as the main force would be brought up against the citadel to divert the defenders.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:12-6)

The following morning a number of volunteers rushed ashore, one Ruy Gonçalves being recorded as the first to land, and Henry followed along with Edward.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:12-6) After a struggle the Muslims were driven from the landing grounds to the city walls. The Portuguese breached into Ceuta but Henry did not allow his squadron of men to rush inside.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:22-7) He kept them by the gates and sent for reinforcements, which were quickly brought up led by Fernandes de Ataíde, who cheered them on.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:22-7) He advanced into urban combat in narrow streets, but eventually the Muslims were routed.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:22-7) The Portuguese scattered for plunder, risked losing the city in a counterattack.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:22-7) Henry's squadron broke a Muslim rally twice, and with seventeen men held a gate on the inner wall between the lower town and the high citadel.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:22-7) Contact was lost between Henry, Peter and the main Portuguese force, and they were reported dead to King John I, though both were found alive towards the evening.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:22-7) Henry held a council with his brothers Edward and Peter, all deciding to assault the citadel the following morning, but after sunset scouts reported that almost all defenders had already evacuated, and the citadel surrendered.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-8)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/04/Porto_April_2019-7.jpg/250px-Porto_April_2019-7.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Porto_April_2019-7.jpg)

Prince Henry at the 1415 [Conquest of Ceuta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conquest_of_Ceuta "Conquest of Ceuta"), considered the beginning of the [Portuguese Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Empire "Portuguese Empire").

Henry was knighted at Ceuta along with his two brothers by King John, who also made them dukes, the first time this title was employed in Portugal.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:02-9) Henry was made Duke of Viseu, appointed governor of the [Order of Christ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_Order_of_Christ "Military Order of Christ"), and made responsible for the provisioning of the newly captured city.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:02-9) Henry became renowned throughout Europe after the capture of Ceuta, and he was invited by the [Pope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papal_States "Papal States"), the [Holy Roman Emperor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Roman_Emperor "Holy Roman Emperor") and the kings of [Castile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Castile "Kingdom of Castile") and [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England "England") to command their armies.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:02-9)

Following this success, in 1416 [Prince Peter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter,_Duke_of_Coimbra "Peter, Duke of Coimbra") left for a [grand tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_tour "Grand tour") across Europe, and his travels were instrumental in stimulating the efforts of his brother Henry.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:1-10) His first destination was the [Holy Land](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Land "Holy Land").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:1-10) From there Pedro proceeded to the [Ottoman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire") court, Babylon, where he was afforded a grand reception, and from there moved on to [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome"), where he met [Pope Martin V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Martin_V "Pope Martin V").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:1-10) He also visited [Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Hungary_(1301%E2%80%931526) "Kingdom of Hungary (1301–1526)"), [Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark "Denmark") and [Venice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_Venice "Republic of Venice"), where he was gifted by the republic a copy of the _[Travels of Marco Polo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Travels\_of\_Marco\_Polo "The Travels of Marco Polo")_, together with a map thought to have been made by Polo himself.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:1-10) He then travelled to England, where he was elected [Knight of the Garter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_Garter "Order of the Garter") on the 22nd of April 1427, and returned to Portugal the following year.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:1-10)

### Relief of Ceuta, 1418

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Prince_Henry_the_Navigator&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Relief of Ceuta, 1418")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b5/Septa_%28Ceuta%29_ca_1572.jpg/250px-Septa_%28Ceuta%29_ca_1572.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Septa_(Ceuta)_ca_1572.jpg)

Ceuta in 1572.

Three years after the conquest of Ceuta, the emir of Granada and the sultan of Fez joined forces to besiege Ceuta by land and sea.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:4-11) The ruler of Granada sent seventy four ships, while the forces of Fez managed to breach into the lower town. The governor of Ceuta Dom Pedro de Meneses dispatched to Portugal a request for aid and Henry was sent to organize a relief expedition from Lisbon, while Edward and Pedro prepared to follow him from Lagos and the rest of the Algarve if need be.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:4-11) The Muslims secured Almina while the galleys of Granada closed in upon the port in the meantime.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:4-11) As the relief fleet commanded by Henry crossed the Straits of Gibraltar it received news of the dire situation in the city.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:4-11) However the sight of the approaching fleet caused panic among the besiegers and by the time it finally reached Ceuta most of the Muslims had already withdrawn.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:4-11)

Henry remained at Ceuta with his forces for two months.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:5-12) While there he planned an attack on Gibraltar on the way to Portugal, but a storm scattered the fleet and the attack was called off.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:5-12) Both expeditions to Ceuta in 1415 and 1418 allowed Henry to gather intelligence on the lands to the south, obtained mainly from Muslim prisoners.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:6-13) They included "news of the passage of merchants from the coasts of [Tunis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunis "Tunis") to [Timbuctoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbuktu "Timbuktu") and to Cantor on the [Gambia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gambia_River "Gambia River"), which inspired him to seek the lands by the way of the sea" but also information of "certain tall palms growing at the mouth of the [Senegal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senegal_River "Senegal River")", obtained from [Sanhaja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanhaja "Sanhaja"), referred to as "tawny moors" or _Azenegues_ by the Portuguese.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:6-13)

In 1419, Henry's father appointed him governor of the province of the [Algarve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algarve "Algarve").

## Resources and income

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Prince_Henry_the_Navigator&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Resources and income")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b2/Arms_of_Henry_of_Portugal%2C_Duke_of_Viseu.svg/250px-Arms_of_Henry_of_Portugal%2C_Duke_of_Viseu.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Arms_of_Henry_of_Portugal,_Duke_of_Viseu.svg)

[Coat of arms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_heraldry "Portuguese heraldry") of Prince Henry as [Duke of Viseu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Viseu "Duke of Viseu"). 

On May 25, 1420, Henry gained appointment as the administrator of the [Order of Christ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_Christ_(Portugal) "Order of Christ (Portugal)"), the Portuguese successor to the [Knights Templar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knights_Templar "Knights Templar"), which had its headquarters at [Tomar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomar "Tomar") in central Portugal.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-Prestage-14) Henry held this position for the remainder of his life, and the Order was an important source of funds for his ambitious plans, especially his persistent attempts to conquer the [Canary Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands "Canary Islands"), which the Portuguese had claimed to have discovered before the year 1346.

Prince [Peter, Duke of Coimbra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter,_Duke_of_Coimbra "Peter, Duke of Coimbra"), had set out on a diplomatic tour of Europe, with an additional charge from Henry to seek out geographic material. Peter returned in 1426 with a world map from Venice.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-Rush-15)

In 1431, Henry donated houses for the _[Estudo Geral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estudo\_Geral "Estudo Geral")_ to teach all the sciences—grammar, logic, rhetoric, arithmetic, music, and astronomy—in what would later become the [University of Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Lisbon "University of Lisbon"). For other subjects like medicine or philosophy, he ordered that each room should be decorated according to the subject taught.

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/98401-Tomar_%2848914397516%29.jpg/250px-98401-Tomar_%2848914397516%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:98401-Tomar_(48914397516).jpg)

Prince Henry ordered construction of the _Paços Henriquinos_ (Henrician Palace) at the [Convent of Christ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convent_of_Christ "Convent of Christ") in [Tomar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomar "Tomar"), to serve as his residence when he was appointed as Governor of the [Order of Christ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_Order_of_Christ "Military Order of Christ") in 1420.

Henry also had other resources. When John I died in 1433, Henry's eldest brother [Edward of Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_of_Portugal "Edward of Portugal") became king. He granted Henry all profits from trading within the areas he discovered as well as the sole right to authorize expeditions beyond [Cape Bojador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Bojador "Cape Bojador"). Henry also held a monopoly on tuna fishing in the [Algarve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algarve "Algarve"). When Edward died eight years later, Henry supported his brother [Peter, Duke of Coimbra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter,_Duke_of_Coimbra "Peter, Duke of Coimbra") for the regency during the minority of Edward's son [Afonso V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_V_of_Portugal "Afonso V of Portugal"), and in return received a confirmation of this levy.

Henry was the main organizer of the disastrous [expedition to Tangier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Tangier_(1437) "Battle of Tangier (1437)") in 1437 against Salah Ben Salah, which ended in Henry's younger brother [Ferdinand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_the_Saint_Prince "Ferdinand the Saint Prince") being given as hostage to guarantee Portuguese promises in the peace agreement. The [Portuguese Cortes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Cortes "Portuguese Cortes") refused to return Ceuta as ransom for Ferdinand, who remained in captivity until his death six years later.

Prince Regent Peter supported Portuguese maritime expansion in the Atlantic Ocean and Africa. Henry promoted the colonization of the [Azores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azores "Azores") during Peter's regency (1439–1448). For most of the latter part of his life, Henry concentrated on his maritime activities and court politics.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-Bradford,_1960-4)

## Vila do Infante and Portuguese exploration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Prince_Henry_the_Navigator&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Vila do Infante and Portuguese exploration")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/Fortaleza_de_Sagres_2_-_11.04.2023.jpg/250px-Fortaleza_de_Sagres_2_-_11.04.2023.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Fortaleza_de_Sagres_2_-_11.04.2023.jpg)

The [Fortress of Sagres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortress_of_Sagres "Fortress of Sagres"), near [Cape St. Vincent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_St._Vincent "Cape St. Vincent") in the [Algarve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algarve "Algarve"), is said to have been the seat of the legendary [Sagres school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sagres_school "Sagres school").

According to [João de Barros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jo%C3%A3o_de_Barros "João de Barros"), in Algarve, Prince Henry the Navigator repopulated a village that he called [Terçanabal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sagres_(Vila_do_Bispo) "Sagres (Vila do Bispo)") (from _terça nabal_ or _tercena nabal_).[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-16) This village was situated in a strategic position for his maritime enterprises and was later called Vila do Infante ("Estate or Town of the Prince").

It is traditionally suggested that Henry gathered at his villa on the [Sagres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sagres_Point "Sagres Point") peninsula a school of navigators and [map-makers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mapmaking "Mapmaking"). However modern historians hold this to be a misconception. He did employ some cartographers to chart the coast of [Mauritania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mauritania "Mauritania") after the voyages he sent there, but there was no center of navigation science or observatory in the modern sense of the word, nor was there an organized navigational center.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-Randles-17)

Referring to Sagres, sixteenth-century Portuguese mathematician and cosmographer [Pedro Nunes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedro_Nunes "Pedro Nunes") remarked, "from it our sailors went out well taught and provided with instruments and rules which all map makers and navigators should know."[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-18)

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3e/Azulejos_Parque_Eduardo_VII-1.jpg/250px-Azulejos_Parque_Eduardo_VII-1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Azulejos_Parque_Eduardo_VII-1.jpg)

"Sagres". Monumental allegorical [azulejos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azulejo "Azulejo") tile panel in Lisbon dedicated to Prince Henry.

The view that Henry's court rapidly grew into the technological base for exploration, with a naval arsenal and an observatory, etc., although repeated in popular culture, has never been established.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-19)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-20)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-21) Henry did possess geographical curiosity, and employed cartographers. [Jehuda Cresques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jehuda_Cresques "Jehuda Cresques"), a noted cartographer, has been said to have accepted an invitation to come to Portugal to make maps for the infante. Prestage makes the argument that the presence of the latter at the Prince's court "probably accounts for the legend of the School of Sagres, which is now discredited."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-Prestage-14)
