# Padrão dos Descobrimentos. Lisbon’s Monument to the Age of Discoveries

2018 By [justmovingaround](https://justmovingaround.com/author/justmovingaround/ "View all posts by justmovingaround")in [History](https://justmovingaround.com/category/history/), [PORTUGAL](https://justmovingaround.com/category/portugal/)Tags: [Discoveries](https://justmovingaround.com/tag/discoveries/), [Portugal](https://justmovingaround.com/tag/portugal/)

The Padrão dos Descobrimentos stands proudly on the banks of the Tagus in Lisbon, a striking tribute to Portugal’s Age of Discoveries. Built in 1960 to honour Prince Henry the Navigator and fellow explorers, the monument captures the spirit of a nation that once led the world across uncharted seas.

Portugal played a central role in the Age of Discoveries, a period during the 15th and 16th centuries when European nations began exploring the world by sea. Portuguese navigators were among the first to venture beyond known horizons, opening maritime routes to Africa, Asia, and the Americas. These voyages not only expanded geographical knowledge but also shaped global trade, culture, and history. To honour their legacy, a monument was erected in Lisbon — the **Padrão dos Descobrimentos**, or Monument to the Discoveries — celebrating the vision and achievements of this remarkable era.

The monument stands in **Belém**, Lisbon, on the northern bank of the **River Tagus**, near the spot from which many of Portugal’s great maritime expeditions once set sail. It commemorates the **Age of Discoveries**, when Portuguese navigators explored the coasts of Africa, Asia and the Americas, establishing Portugal as a major global power. It was first created as a temporary structure in **1940** for the **Portuguese World Exhibition**. Due to its popularity, it was rebuilt in stone and inaugurated in **1960**, marking the **500th anniversary of the death of Prince Henry the Navigator** (_Infante Dom Henrique_). Henry stands at the front of the monument holding a model of a caravel, symbolising leadership and exploration. At the base of the monument, on the square, is a large **mosaic wind rose and world map**, a gift from South Africa, illustrating the routes taken by Portuguese explorers across the globe. The Padrão dos Descobrimentos serves as both a **symbol of national pride** and a **reminder of Portugal’s complex maritime legacy**.

[![Image 1: Padrão dos Descobrimentos](https://i0.wp.com/justmovingaround.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/01/jma_discoveries.jpg?ssl=1)](https://i0.wp.com/justmovingaround.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/01/jma_discoveries.jpg?ssl=1)

Historical figures important for the Portuguese discoveries like**Vasco da Gama**,**Magellan**,**Cabral,**and others follow**Prince Henry the Navigator**. He is standing at the prow, holding a small vessel in hand.Padrão dos Descobrimentos or simply Discoveries Monument in Lisbon, Portugal.

Advertisement

The monument itself is shaped like the prow of a ship and rises **52 metres high**. Behind Henry, arranged on both sides, are **33 figures** representing key people from the Age of Discoveries, including **explorers, captains, missionaries, scientists, cartographers, chroniclers, and members of the royal family** – all of whom played significant roles in Portugal’s maritime expansion. They all are led be **Prince Henry the Navigator**.

Prince Henry the Navigator(1394-1460), or to be precise**Infante Henrique of Portugal, Duke of Viseu**was a son of a Portuguese king. The nickname Navigator was given to him centuries after his death to underline his leading role for the European Age of Discoveries. But**in fact, he was never a sailor**.**He was an enthusiast of discovering new territories and new trade routes skilled enough to organize and finance the explorations**. He paid cartographers from Italian cities that already traded with the Middle East and Asia (using land routes) to draw the most actual world maps (for that time, of course). He also set up an academy that trained sailors. He helped to claim new territories for the Portuguese crown and promoted trade with Africa and India. At first, the funds for explorations came mainly from the Military Order of Christ (the successors of Templars in Portugal, with the seat in Tomar). Later on, his elderly brother, the king of Portugal, granted him a share in trade profits, which he, in turn, used for funding new undertakings. The discoveries, although detrimental for the native populations in newly claimed territories, brought for years welfare to the Portuguese crown.

On the monument on his left hand side (people you can see on my photo), there are: **Afonso V of Portugal** (king of Portugal, known as “the African” for his military campaigns in Morocco), **Vasco da Gama** (navigator, discovered the sea route to India in 1498), **Afonso Baldaia** (navigator, early explorer of the West African coast under Prince Henry the Navigator), **Pedro Álvares Cabral** (navigator, officially discovered Brazil in 1500), **Ferdinand Magellan (Fernão de Magalhães)** (navigator, led the first circumnavigation of the globe, although he died during the voyage), **Nicolau Coelho** (navigator, accompanied Vasco da Gama and Cabral on their voyages to India and Brazil), **Gaspar Corte-Real** (navigator, explored the Labrador Peninsula in present-day Canada), **Martim Afonso de Sousa** (navigator, led early colonizing efforts in Brazil and founded São Vicente), **João de Barros** (chronicler and historian, wrote detailed accounts of Portuguese discoveries and conquests), **Estêvão da Gama** (captain, son of Vasco da Gama, involved in expeditions in India), **Bartolomeu Dias** (navigator, first to sail around the Cape of Good Hope in 1488), **Diogo Cão** (navigator, explored the west coast of Africa and reached the Congo River), **António de Abreu** (navigator, led an expedition to the Spice Islands, present-day Indonesia), **Afonso de Albuquerque** (viceroy of India and governor, key figure in establishing Portuguese dominance in the Indian Ocean), **Saint Francis Xavier (São Francisco Xavier)** (missionary and evangelizer, co-founder of the Jesuits, active in Asia), **Cristóvão da Gama** (captain, son of Vasco da Gama, led a military expedition to Ethiopia and died in battle).

On his right hand side, there are: **Infante D. Fernando (the Holy Prince)** (son of King João I of Portugal, participated in the failed Tangier expedition, captured and died in captivity, later revered as a martyr),  
**João Gonçalves Zarco** (navigator, co-discoverer of the Madeira archipelago and early colonizer), **Gil Eanes** (navigator, first to successfully round Cape Bojador in 1434, breaking a major psychological barrier of maritime exploration), **Pêro de Alenquer** (navigator and pilot, took part in Bartolomeu Dias’s and Vasco da Gama’s expeditions), **Pedro Nunes** (mathematician and cosmographer, advanced navigation science and invented the nonius for precise measurements), **Pêro Escobar** (navigator and pilot, participated in the discovery of the Gulf of Guinea and the islands of São Tomé and Príncipe),  
**Jácome de Maiorca** (cosmographer, mapmaker from Majorca known for contributing to nautical cartography in Portugal), **Pêro da Covilhã** (traveller and diplomat, sent on a secret mission to the East before the sea route to India was discovered, reached Ethiopia), **Gomes Eanes de Zurara** (chronicler, wrote the _Crónica da Guiné_, detailing early Portuguese exploration and conquests in Africa), **Nuno Gonçalves** (painter, attributed with the _Saint Vincent Panels_, considered masterpieces of Portuguese art), **Luís Vaz de Camões** (epic poet, author of _Os Lusíadas_, Portugal’s national literary epic glorifying the Age of Discoveries), **Friar Henrique de Coimbra** (Franciscan missionary, celebrated the first mass in Brazil with Cabral’s fleet), **Friar Gonçalo de Carvalho** (Dominican friar, missionary who traveled to Asia and was involved in evangelization efforts), **Fernão Mendes Pinto** (writer and adventurer, author of _Peregrinação_, chronicling his travels in Asia with a mix of fact and fiction), **Queen Philippa of Lancaster (Dona Filipa de Lencastre)** (English-born queen of Portugal, wife of King João I, mother of the “Illustrious Generation” of princes), **Infante D. Pedro, Duke of Coimbra** (son of King João I, regent of Portugal, humanist, traveler, and promoter of culture and knowledge).

# Padrão dos Descobrimentos. Lisbon’s Monument to the Age of Discoveries

2018 By [justmovingaround](https://justmovingaround.com/author/justmovingaround/ "View all posts by justmovingaround")in [History](https://justmovingaround.com/category/history/), [PORTUGAL](https://justmovingaround.com/category/portugal/)Tags: [Discoveries](https://justmovingaround.com/tag/discoveries/), [Portugal](https://justmovingaround.com/tag/portugal/)

The Padrão dos Descobrimentos stands proudly on the banks of the Tagus in Lisbon, a striking tribute to Portugal’s Age of Discoveries. Built in 1960 to honour Prince Henry the Navigator and fellow explorers, the monument captures the spirit of a nation that once led the world across uncharted seas.

Portugal played a central role in the Age of Discoveries, a period during the 15th and 16th centuries when European nations began exploring the world by sea. Portuguese navigators were among the first to venture beyond known horizons, opening maritime routes to Africa, Asia, and the Americas. These voyages not only expanded geographical knowledge but also shaped global trade, culture, and history. To honour their legacy, a monument was erected in Lisbon — the **Padrão dos Descobrimentos**, or Monument to the Discoveries — celebrating the vision and achievements of this remarkable era.

The monument stands in **Belém**, Lisbon, on the northern bank of the **River Tagus**, near the spot from which many of Portugal’s great maritime expeditions once set sail. It commemorates the **Age of Discoveries**, when Portuguese navigators explored the coasts of Africa, Asia and the Americas, establishing Portugal as a major global power. It was first created as a temporary structure in **1940** for the **Portuguese World Exhibition**. Due to its popularity, it was rebuilt in stone and inaugurated in **1960**, marking the **500th anniversary of the death of Prince Henry the Navigator** (_Infante Dom Henrique_). Henry stands at the front of the monument holding a model of a caravel, symbolising leadership and exploration. At the base of the monument, on the square, is a large **mosaic wind rose and world map**, a gift from South Africa, illustrating the routes taken by Portuguese explorers across the globe. The Padrão dos Descobrimentos serves as both a **symbol of national pride** and a **reminder of Portugal’s complex maritime legacy**.

[![Image 1: Padrão dos Descobrimentos](https://i0.wp.com/justmovingaround.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/01/jma_discoveries.jpg?ssl=1)](https://i0.wp.com/justmovingaround.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/01/jma_discoveries.jpg?ssl=1)

Historical figures important for the Portuguese discoveries like**Vasco da Gama**,**Magellan**,**Cabral,**and others follow**Prince Henry the Navigator**. He is standing at the prow, holding a small vessel in hand.Padrão dos Descobrimentos or simply Discoveries Monument in Lisbon, Portugal.

Advertisement

The monument itself is shaped like the prow of a ship and rises **52 metres high**. Behind Henry, arranged on both sides, are **33 figures** representing key people from the Age of Discoveries, including **explorers, captains, missionaries, scientists, cartographers, chroniclers, and members of the royal family** – all of whom played significant roles in Portugal’s maritime expansion. They all are led be **Prince Henry the Navigator**.

Prince Henry the Navigator(1394-1460), or to be precise**Infante Henrique of Portugal, Duke of Viseu**was a son of a Portuguese king. The nickname Navigator was given to him centuries after his death to underline his leading role for the European Age of Discoveries. But**in fact, he was never a sailor**.**He was an enthusiast of discovering new territories and new trade routes skilled enough to organize and finance the explorations**. He paid cartographers from Italian cities that already traded with the Middle East and Asia (using land routes) to draw the most actual world maps (for that time, of course). He also set up an academy that trained sailors. He helped to claim new territories for the Portuguese crown and promoted trade with Africa and India. At first, the funds for explorations came mainly from the Military Order of Christ (the successors of Templars in Portugal, with the seat in Tomar). Later on, his elderly brother, the king of Portugal, granted him a share in trade profits, which he, in turn, used for funding new undertakings. The discoveries, although detrimental for the native populations in newly claimed territories, brought for years welfare to the Portuguese crown.

On the monument on his left hand side (people you can see on my photo), there are: **Afonso V of Portugal** (king of Portugal, known as “the African” for his military campaigns in Morocco), **Vasco da Gama** (navigator, discovered the sea route to India in 1498), **Afonso Baldaia** (navigator, early explorer of the West African coast under Prince Henry the Navigator), **Pedro Álvares Cabral** (navigator, officially discovered Brazil in 1500), **Ferdinand Magellan (Fernão de Magalhães)** (navigator, led the first circumnavigation of the globe, although he died during the voyage), **Nicolau Coelho** (navigator, accompanied Vasco da Gama and Cabral on their voyages to India and Brazil), **Gaspar Corte-Real** (navigator, explored the Labrador Peninsula in present-day Canada), **Martim Afonso de Sousa** (navigator, led early colonizing efforts in Brazil and founded São Vicente), **João de Barros** (chronicler and historian, wrote detailed accounts of Portuguese discoveries and conquests), **Estêvão da Gama** (captain, son of Vasco da Gama, involved in expeditions in India), **Bartolomeu Dias** (navigator, first to sail around the Cape of Good Hope in 1488), **Diogo Cão** (navigator, explored the west coast of Africa and reached the Congo River), **António de Abreu** (navigator, led an expedition to the Spice Islands, present-day Indonesia), **Afonso de Albuquerque** (viceroy of India and governor, key figure in establishing Portuguese dominance in the Indian Ocean), **Saint Francis Xavier (São Francisco Xavier)** (missionary and evangelizer, co-founder of the Jesuits, active in Asia), **Cristóvão da Gama** (captain, son of Vasco da Gama, led a military expedition to Ethiopia and died in battle).

On his right hand side, there are: **Infante D. Fernando (the Holy Prince)** (son of King João I of Portugal, participated in the failed Tangier expedition, captured and died in captivity, later revered as a martyr),  
**João Gonçalves Zarco** (navigator, co-discoverer of the Madeira archipelago and early colonizer), **Gil Eanes** (navigator, first to successfully round Cape Bojador in 1434, breaking a major psychological barrier of maritime exploration), **Pêro de Alenquer** (navigator and pilot, took part in Bartolomeu Dias’s and Vasco da Gama’s expeditions), **Pedro Nunes** (mathematician and cosmographer, advanced navigation science and invented the nonius for precise measurements), **Pêro Escobar** (navigator and pilot, participated in the discovery of the Gulf of Guinea and the islands of São Tomé and Príncipe),  
**Jácome de Maiorca** (cosmographer, mapmaker from Majorca known for contributing to nautical cartography in Portugal), **Pêro da Covilhã** (traveller and diplomat, sent on a secret mission to the East before the sea route to India was discovered, reached Ethiopia), **Gomes Eanes de Zurara** (chronicler, wrote the _Crónica da Guiné_, detailing early Portuguese exploration and conquests in Africa), **Nuno Gonçalves** (painter, attributed with the _Saint Vincent Panels_, considered masterpieces of Portuguese art), **Luís Vaz de Camões** (epic poet, author of _Os Lusíadas_, Portugal’s national literary epic glorifying the Age of Discoveries), **Friar Henrique de Coimbra** (Franciscan missionary, celebrated the first mass in Brazil with Cabral’s fleet), **Friar Gonçalo de Carvalho** (Dominican friar, missionary who traveled to Asia and was involved in evangelization efforts), **Fernão Mendes Pinto** (writer and adventurer, author of _Peregrinação_, chronicling his travels in Asia with a mix of fact and fiction), **Queen Philippa of Lancaster (Dona Filipa de Lencastre)** (English-born queen of Portugal, wife of King João I, mother of the “Illustrious Generation” of princes), **Infante D. Pedro, Duke of Coimbra** (son of King João I, regent of Portugal, humanist, traveler, and promoter of culture and knowledge).

# Treasures from the Portuguese Maritime Museum

## The Museum has a great collection of more than 20.000 objects, of which 2500 are in exhibition, so this catalog represents a small sample of what you can find in the Museum.

Planispheric map (1970) by Workshops of the Maritime Museum and Alberto Cutileiro**Portuguese Maritime Museum, a world of discoveries**

### Planispheric map

This map occupies the furthest wall at the entrance of the Maritime Museum, showing the main voyages accomplished by Portuguese navigators as well as the meridian defined by the “Treaty of Tordesillas”.

Statue of Prince Henry "the Navigator" (c. 1901 - c. 2000) by Leopoldo Neves de Almeida**Portuguese Maritime Museum, a world of discoveries**

### Statue of Prince Henry "the Navigator"

Positioned at the center of the Maritime Museum's entrance and surrounded by several Portuguese explorers that commenced the Portuguese Atlantic adventure,Prince Henrique’s “the Navigator” statue stands as a testament to his role as one of the first and most important proponents of the Portuguese Discoveries.

Lateen Rigged Caravel (1956) by Workshops of the Maritime Museum**Portuguese Maritime Museum, a world of discoveries**

### Lateen Rigged Caravel

The advances in Portuguese shipbuilding during the Early Modern period were key to the success of the exploratory voyages completed in what became known as the Discoveries. Is usually seen as the main example in said advances, becoming a symbol of Portuguese Discoveries.

Archangel St. Raphael (1947) by No info**Portuguese Maritime Museum, a world of discoveries**

### Archangel St. Raphael

Sculpted in wood, this statuette was part of one of the most important voyages in both Portuguese and global maritime history: the discovery of the sea route between Europe and India, in 1498.It is the most important material testimony of this trip, commanded by Vasco da Gama.

Astrolabe "Atocha III" (1605) by Agostinho de Goes Raposo**Portuguese Maritime Museum, a world of discoveries**

### Astrolabe Atocha III

The development of astronomical navigation was fundamental for increasing the safety of ocean voyages undertaken by the Portuguese in the period of the Discoveries. Currently, the Maritime Museum has one of the richest collections of nautical astrolabes on display in the world.

1502 Anonymous Planisphere, the "Cantino's Map" (1502) by Anonymous**Portuguese Maritime Museum, a world of discoveries**

### 1502 Anonymous Planisphere, the Cantino's Map

Copy of the original found in the Biblioteca Estense in Modena, Italy. Through this map, the scope of the Portuguese Discoveries is clear, showing how in just under 100 years the Portuguese had increased their geographical knowledge to the point of creating a world map in which, the represented lands, people, fauna and flora, are recognizable by today's standards.

Indiamen "Madre Deus" (2000) by António Marques da Silva and Ferdinando Oliveira Simões**Portuguese Maritime Museum, a world of discoveries**

### Indiamen Madre Deus

This was the largest Portuguese “Nau” (Indiaman) to ever complete the India Run and one of the largest ships in the world when it was built. On its final voyage, was captured by English Pirates who, fascinated by the sheer magnitude of it, sailed the ship back do England.

Painting of the "Naval Battle at Cape St. Vicente" (1842) by Morel Fatio**Portuguese Maritime Museum, a world of discoveries**

### Painting of the Naval Battle at Cape St. Vincent

On July 5th, 1833, during the Portuguese Liberal Wars, a naval battle took place off the coast of the Cape St. Vincent, in the south of Portugal, between the liberals and the absolutists. It was the last battle fought exclusively between portuguese sailing ships.

Frigate "D. Fernando II e Glória" (c. 1901 - c. 2000) by Seixas Workshop**Portuguese Maritime Museum, a world of discoveries**

### Frigate Dom Fernando II e Glória

Built in the royal shipyard in Daman, in the former Estado da Índia, between 1832 and 1845, was the last solely wind-powered vessel of the Portuguese Navy and was the last Indiaman to complete the India Run that linked Portugal to the Indian Ocean for the three centuries previously.

Cruiser "Adamastor" (c. 1901 - c. 2000) by Seixas Workshop**Portuguese Maritime Museum, a world of discoveries**

### Cruiser Adamastor

Built at the Fratelli Orlando Shipyard, in Livorno, it was a powerfully armed warship, which appeared at the end of the 19th century, as result of the need to renew the Portuguese naval fleet. It played a key role in several important periods in the Portuguese history, such as the establishment of the Republic.

Flag of the Republican Revolution (1910) by No info**Portuguese Maritime Museum, a world of discoveries**

### Flag of the Republican Revolution

Republican flag hoisted aboard the cruiser “Adamastor”, act that gave the signal for the beginning of the revolution. The Portuguese Republic was proclaimed on October 5, 1910, putting an end to the monarchical regime that had been in force since the beginning of nationality.

Minesweeper "Augusto de Castilho" lifeboat (1918) by No info**Portuguese Maritime Museum, a world of discoveries**

### Minesweeper Augusto de Castilho lifeboat

Lifeboat that carried the Augusto de Castilho survivors from the fight against the german submarine U-139. Combat occurred on October 14, 1918, where the Commander of "Augusto Castilho", Lieutenant Carvalho de Araújo, as well as six other crew elements lost their lives. Lothar von Arnaud de la Perière commanded the U-139, considered the best submariner of all times.

Launch "Vega" (1965) by Workshops of the Maritime Museum**Portuguese Maritime Museum, a world of discoveries**

### Launch Vega

Commissioned by the Portuguese Navy on the 10th of December 1959, this launch had an important role in the Navy’s final engagements in India, during the Indian invasion of Portuguese Diu, in 1961.

"Cacilheiro" boat "Boa Viagem" (c. 1901 - c. 2000) by Seixas Workshop**Portuguese Maritime Museum, a world of discoveries**

### Cacilheiro boat Boa Viagem

Until recently, water streams were the main forms of communication between different peoples and places. One of the models that best represents this aspect is the “Cacilheiro” dinghy, an important vessel to the lives of the people in the Tagus estuary – so much so that its name has been passed down to the current ferries in the river.

Schooner "Argus" (1938) by Amadeu Marques and Luís António Marques**Portuguese Maritime Museum, a world of discoveries**

### Schooner Argus

Built in 1938 at the Haan Oerlmans shipyards, in Netherlands, for “Parceria Geral de Pescarias Ltdª”, the “Argus” lugger represents the continuation of the construction of metallic ships for long-distance fishing in Portugal, namely, one of the foods that is still present on Portuguese tables today, the codfish.

"Lancha" ou "Galeão" da Nazaré (c. 1901 - c. 2000) by Seixas Workshop**Portuguese Maritime Museum, a world of discoveries**

### Lancha ou Galeão da Nazaré

Coastal fishing is a type of fishing that is carried out, as a rule, with the coast in sight, this being a very old type of fishing that predates the very existence of Portugal, which remains today and is part of the Portuguese tradition.

The Tagus "Muleta" (c. 1901 - c. 2000) by No info**Portuguese Maritime Museum, a world of discoveries**

### The Tagus Muleta

It appeared in the 17th century and was a fishing vessel used by fishermen from the estuaries on the south bank of the Tagus River (Seixal, Barreiro and Moita), who crossed the bar to cast nets between Cabo da Rocha and Cabo Espichel.

Royal Chambers of the Yatch "Amélia" (1901) by Ramage & Ferguson**Portuguese Maritime Museum, a world of discoveries**

### Royal Chambers of the Yacht Amélia

This room is considered to be one of the extravagant spaces of the Maritime Museum, dedicated to the royal chambers of the yacht “Amélia”, the luxurious rooms of king Carlos and queen-consort Amélie of Orleans, salvaged from the yacht when it was paid off by the Navy in 1938.

### King's Chamber

### Queen's Chamber

Royal Brigantine (1780) by Torcato José Clavina**Portuguese Maritime Museum, a world of discoveries**

### Royal Brigantine

One of the most imposing objects in the Barge Pavilion and one of the most important elements of the collection of the Maritime Museum, this royal vessel built at the end of the 18th century helps to understand the strong connection that has always existed between the royal families and the sea.

Royal Brigantine (1780) by Torcato José Clavina**Portuguese Maritime Museum, a world of discoveries**

View of the interior of the Royal Bergantim.

Royal Brigantine (1780) by Torcato José Clavina**Portuguese Maritime Museum, a world of discoveries**

Other perspective of the interior of the Royal Bergantim’s Royal Chamber.

Royal Brigantine (1780) by Torcato José Clavina**Portuguese Maritime Museum, a world of discoveries**

View of the interior of the Royal Bergantim’s Royal Chamber.

Seaplane "Fairey III D" «Santa Cruz» (1921) by Fairey Aviation Company Limited**Portuguese Maritime Museum, a world of discoveries**

### Seaplane Fairey III D «Santa Cruz»

It was the third seaplane of the “Fairey” type (No. 17) used in the First Air Crossing of the South Atlantic, starring Gago Coutinho and Sacadura Cabral. It was transported from Lisbon to Fernando de Noronha Island in June 1922, thus completing the Air Crossing between Lisbon an Rio de Janeiro. Upon completion of the trip, was baptized "Santa Cruz".

**Prince Henry the Navigator**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-1) (4 March 1394 – 13 December 1460), was a [Portuguese prince](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infante_of_Portugal "Infante of Portugal"), a central figure in the early days of the [Portuguese Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Empire "Portuguese Empire") and often credited as one of the main initiators of the [Age of Discovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Discovery "Age of Discovery"). Henry was the third child of King [John I of Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_I_of_Portugal "John I of Portugal"), who founded the [House of Aviz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Aviz "House of Aviz").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-2)

Utilising the new [caravel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caravel "Caravel") ship, Henry directed the early development of Portuguese exploration and maritime trade with other continents through the systematic exploration of Western Africa, the islands of the Atlantic Ocean, and the search for new routes. He supported his father in the 1415 [conquest of Ceuta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_conquest_of_Ceuta "Portuguese conquest of Ceuta"), a Muslim port on the North African coast across the [Straits of Gibraltar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straits_of_Gibraltar "Straits of Gibraltar") from the [Iberian Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberian_Peninsula "Iberian Peninsula"). Regarded as the patron of [Portuguese discoveries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_discoveries "Portuguese discoveries"), he died on 13 November 1460 in Vila do Bispo in the [Algarve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algarve "Algarve").

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Prince_Henry_the_Navigator&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/21/Casa_do_Infante_%28Porto%29.JPG/250px-Casa_do_Infante_%28Porto%29.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Casa_do_Infante_(Porto).JPG)

The [Casa do Infante](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casa_do_Infante "Casa do Infante"), in [Porto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porto "Porto"), is traditionally considered Prince Henry's birthplace.

Henry was the third surviving son of [King John I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_I_of_Portugal "John I of Portugal") and his wife [Philippa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippa_of_Lancaster "Philippa of Lancaster"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-mariners-3) sister of [King Henry IV of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_IV_of_England "Henry IV of England"). He was baptized in [Porto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porto "Porto"), and may have been born there, probably when the royal couple was living in the city's old mint, now called [Casa do Infante](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casa_do_Infante "Casa do Infante") (Prince's House), or in the region nearby. Another possibility is that he was born at the Monastery of Leça do Balio, in [Leça da Palmeira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_of_Le%C3%A7a_da_Palmeira "Fort of Leça da Palmeira"), during the same period of the royal couple's residence in the city of Porto.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-Bradford,_1960-4)

As early as 1410 or 1412, Henry had commissioned his captains to explore the coasts beyond [Cape Non](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Chaunar "Cape Chaunar"), which was considered the limit of the known and charted world in Europe together with [Cape Bojador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Bojador "Cape Bojador").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:0-5) Little is known of these expeditions, however.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:0-5)

### The conquest of Ceuta, 1415

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Prince_Henry_the_Navigator&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: The conquest of Ceuta, 1415")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bc/Africa_Portuguese_Empire_1342-1801.png/250px-Africa_Portuguese_Empire_1342-1801.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Africa_Portuguese_Empire_1342-1801.png)

Portuguese presence and exploration in Africa and middle east -1415 - 1801

Henry was 21 when he participated in [an expedition to capture the Moorish port city of Ceuta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conquest_of_Ceuta "Conquest of Ceuta") in northern [Morocco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morocco "Morocco"). Henry was made responsible for recruiting troops and ships in northern Portugal and assemble them at Porto before joining the main fleet en route to Ceuta. At Ceuta, he anchored his ships off the lower part of the town, and on the 15th of August king John rowed through the fleet to inspect it as the attack was to take place the following morning.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:12-6) Henry was said to have claimed and been granted the right to be the first to land. The quays were expected to be devoid of defenders as the main force would be brought up against the citadel to divert the defenders.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:12-6)

The following morning a number of volunteers rushed ashore, one Ruy Gonçalves being recorded as the first to land, and Henry followed along with Edward.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:12-6) After a struggle the Muslims were driven from the landing grounds to the city walls. The Portuguese breached into Ceuta but Henry did not allow his squadron of men to rush inside.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:22-7) He kept them by the gates and sent for reinforcements, which were quickly brought up led by Fernandes de Ataíde, who cheered them on.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:22-7) He advanced into urban combat in narrow streets, but eventually the Muslims were routed.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:22-7) The Portuguese scattered for plunder, risked losing the city in a counterattack.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:22-7) Henry's squadron broke a Muslim rally twice, and with seventeen men held a gate on the inner wall between the lower town and the high citadel.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:22-7) Contact was lost between Henry, Peter and the main Portuguese force, and they were reported dead to King John I, though both were found alive towards the evening.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:22-7) Henry held a council with his brothers Edward and Peter, all deciding to assault the citadel the following morning, but after sunset scouts reported that almost all defenders had already evacuated, and the citadel surrendered.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-8)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/04/Porto_April_2019-7.jpg/250px-Porto_April_2019-7.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Porto_April_2019-7.jpg)

Prince Henry at the 1415 [Conquest of Ceuta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conquest_of_Ceuta "Conquest of Ceuta"), considered the beginning of the [Portuguese Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Empire "Portuguese Empire").

Henry was knighted at Ceuta along with his two brothers by King John, who also made them dukes, the first time this title was employed in Portugal.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:02-9) Henry was made Duke of Viseu, appointed governor of the [Order of Christ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_Order_of_Christ "Military Order of Christ"), and made responsible for the provisioning of the newly captured city.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:02-9) Henry became renowned throughout Europe after the capture of Ceuta, and he was invited by the [Pope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papal_States "Papal States"), the [Holy Roman Emperor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Roman_Emperor "Holy Roman Emperor") and the kings of [Castile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Castile "Kingdom of Castile") and [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England "England") to command their armies.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:02-9)

Following this success, in 1416 [Prince Peter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter,_Duke_of_Coimbra "Peter, Duke of Coimbra") left for a [grand tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_tour "Grand tour") across Europe, and his travels were instrumental in stimulating the efforts of his brother Henry.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:1-10) His first destination was the [Holy Land](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Land "Holy Land").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:1-10) From there Pedro proceeded to the [Ottoman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire") court, Babylon, where he was afforded a grand reception, and from there moved on to [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome"), where he met [Pope Martin V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Martin_V "Pope Martin V").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:1-10) He also visited [Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Hungary_(1301%E2%80%931526) "Kingdom of Hungary (1301–1526)"), [Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark "Denmark") and [Venice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_Venice "Republic of Venice"), where he was gifted by the republic a copy of the _[Travels of Marco Polo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Travels\_of\_Marco\_Polo "The Travels of Marco Polo")_, together with a map thought to have been made by Polo himself.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:1-10) He then travelled to England, where he was elected [Knight of the Garter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_Garter "Order of the Garter") on the 22nd of April 1427, and returned to Portugal the following year.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:1-10)

### Relief of Ceuta, 1418

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Prince_Henry_the_Navigator&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Relief of Ceuta, 1418")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b5/Septa_%28Ceuta%29_ca_1572.jpg/250px-Septa_%28Ceuta%29_ca_1572.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Septa_(Ceuta)_ca_1572.jpg)

Ceuta in 1572.

Three years after the conquest of Ceuta, the emir of Granada and the sultan of Fez joined forces to besiege Ceuta by land and sea.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:4-11) The ruler of Granada sent seventy four ships, while the forces of Fez managed to breach into the lower town. The governor of Ceuta Dom Pedro de Meneses dispatched to Portugal a request for aid and Henry was sent to organize a relief expedition from Lisbon, while Edward and Pedro prepared to follow him from Lagos and the rest of the Algarve if need be.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:4-11) The Muslims secured Almina while the galleys of Granada closed in upon the port in the meantime.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:4-11) As the relief fleet commanded by Henry crossed the Straits of Gibraltar it received news of the dire situation in the city.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:4-11) However the sight of the approaching fleet caused panic among the besiegers and by the time it finally reached Ceuta most of the Muslims had already withdrawn.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:4-11)

Henry remained at Ceuta with his forces for two months.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:5-12) While there he planned an attack on Gibraltar on the way to Portugal, but a storm scattered the fleet and the attack was called off.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:5-12) Both expeditions to Ceuta in 1415 and 1418 allowed Henry to gather intelligence on the lands to the south, obtained mainly from Muslim prisoners.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:6-13) They included "news of the passage of merchants from the coasts of [Tunis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunis "Tunis") to [Timbuctoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbuktu "Timbuktu") and to Cantor on the [Gambia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gambia_River "Gambia River"), which inspired him to seek the lands by the way of the sea" but also information of "certain tall palms growing at the mouth of the [Senegal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senegal_River "Senegal River")", obtained from [Sanhaja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanhaja "Sanhaja"), referred to as "tawny moors" or _Azenegues_ by the Portuguese.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:6-13)

In 1419, Henry's father appointed him governor of the province of the [Algarve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algarve "Algarve").

On May 25, 1420, Henry gained appointment as the administrator of the [Order of Christ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_Christ_(Portugal) "Order of Christ (Portugal)"), the Portuguese successor to the [Knights Templar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knights_Templar "Knights Templar"), which had its headquarters at [Tomar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomar "Tomar") in central Portugal.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-Prestage-14) Henry held this position for the remainder of his life, and the Order was an important source of funds for his ambitious plans, especially his persistent attempts to conquer the [Canary Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands "Canary Islands"), which the Portuguese had claimed to have discovered before the year 1346.

Prince [Peter, Duke of Coimbra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter,_Duke_of_Coimbra "Peter, Duke of Coimbra"), had set out on a diplomatic tour of Europe, with an additional charge from Henry to seek out geographic material. Peter returned in 1426 with a world map from Venice.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-Rush-15)

In 1431, Henry donated houses for the _[Estudo Geral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estudo\_Geral "Estudo Geral")_ to teach all the sciences—grammar, logic, rhetoric, arithmetic, music, and astronomy—in what would later become the [University of Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Lisbon "University of Lisbon"). For other subjects like medicine or philosophy, he ordered that each room should be decorated according to the subject taught.

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/98401-Tomar_%2848914397516%29.jpg/250px-98401-Tomar_%2848914397516%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:98401-Tomar_(48914397516).jpg)

Prince Henry ordered construction of the _Paços Henriquinos_ (Henrician Palace) at the [Convent of Christ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convent_of_Christ "Convent of Christ") in [Tomar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomar "Tomar"), to serve as his residence when he was appointed as Governor of the [Order of Christ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_Order_of_Christ "Military Order of Christ") in 1420.

Henry also had other resources. When John I died in 1433, Henry's eldest brother [Edward of Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_of_Portugal "Edward of Portugal") became king. He granted Henry all profits from trading within the areas he discovered as well as the sole right to authorize expeditions beyond [Cape Bojador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Bojador "Cape Bojador"). Henry also held a monopoly on tuna fishing in the [Algarve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algarve "Algarve"). When Edward died eight years later, Henry supported his brother [Peter, Duke of Coimbra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter,_Duke_of_Coimbra "Peter, Duke of Coimbra") for the regency during the minority of Edward's son [Afonso V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_V_of_Portugal "Afonso V of Portugal"), and in return received a confirmation of this levy.

Henry was the main organizer of the disastrous [expedition to Tangier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Tangier_(1437) "Battle of Tangier (1437)") in 1437 against Salah Ben Salah, which ended in Henry's younger brother [Ferdinand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_the_Saint_Prince "Ferdinand the Saint Prince") being given as hostage to guarantee Portuguese promises in the peace agreement. The [Portuguese Cortes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Cortes "Portuguese Cortes") refused to return Ceuta as ransom for Ferdinand, who remained in captivity until his death six years later.

Prince Regent Peter supported Portuguese maritime expansion in the Atlantic Ocean and Africa. Henry promoted the colonization of the [Azores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azores "Azores") during Peter's regency (1439–1448). For most of the latter part of his life, Henry concentrated on his maritime activities and court politics.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-Bradford,_1960-4)

## Vila do Infante and Portuguese exploration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Prince_Henry_the_Navigator&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Vila do Infante and Portuguese exploration")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/Fortaleza_de_Sagres_2_-_11.04.2023.jpg/250px-Fortaleza_de_Sagres_2_-_11.04.2023.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Fortaleza_de_Sagres_2_-_11.04.2023.jpg)

The [Fortress of Sagres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortress_of_Sagres "Fortress of Sagres"), near [Cape St. Vincent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_St._Vincent "Cape St. Vincent") in the [Algarve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algarve "Algarve"), is said to have been the seat of the legendary [Sagres school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sagres_school "Sagres school").

According to [João de Barros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jo%C3%A3o_de_Barros "João de Barros"), in Algarve, Prince Henry the Navigator repopulated a village that he called [Terçanabal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sagres_(Vila_do_Bispo) "Sagres (Vila do Bispo)") (from _terça nabal_ or _tercena nabal_).[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-16) This village was situated in a strategic position for his maritime enterprises and was later called Vila do Infante ("Estate or Town of the Prince").

It is traditionally suggested that Henry gathered at his villa on the [Sagres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sagres_Point "Sagres Point") peninsula a school of navigators and [map-makers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mapmaking "Mapmaking"). However modern historians hold this to be a misconception. He did employ some cartographers to chart the coast of [Mauritania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mauritania "Mauritania") after the voyages he sent there, but there was no center of navigation science or observatory in the modern sense of the word, nor was there an organized navigational center.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-Randles-17)

Referring to Sagres, sixteenth-century Portuguese mathematician and cosmographer [Pedro Nunes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedro_Nunes "Pedro Nunes") remarked, "from it our sailors went out well taught and provided with instruments and rules which all map makers and navigators should know."[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-18)

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3e/Azulejos_Parque_Eduardo_VII-1.jpg/250px-Azulejos_Parque_Eduardo_VII-1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Azulejos_Parque_Eduardo_VII-1.jpg)

"Sagres". Monumental allegorical [azulejos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azulejo "Azulejo") tile panel in Lisbon dedicated to Prince Henry.

The view that Henry's court rapidly grew into the technological base for exploration, with a naval arsenal and an observatory, etc., although repeated in popular culture, has never been established.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-19)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-20)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-21) Henry did possess geographical curiosity, and employed cartographers. [Jehuda Cresques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jehuda_Cresques "Jehuda Cresques"), a noted cartographer, has been said to have accepted an invitation to come to Portugal to make maps for the infante. Prestage makes the argument that the presence of the latter at the Prince's court "probably accounts for the legend of the School of Sagres, which is now discredited."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-Prestage-14)

## Henry's explorations

Map depicting Atlantic winds (green), currents (blue) and approximate Portuguese sailing routes (red) utilizing the _[Volta do mar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volta\_do\_mar "Volta do mar")_ technique, perfected under Prince Henry.

Henry began to explore the coast of Africa, most of which was unknown to Europeans. His objectives included finding the source of the West African gold trade and the legendary Christian kingdom of [Prester John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prester_John "Prester John"), and stopping the pirate attacks on the Portuguese coast.

At that time, the cargo ships of the Mediterranean were too slow and heavy to undertake such voyages. Under Henry's direction, a new and much lighter ship was developed, the [caravel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caravel "Caravel"), which could sail farther and faster.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-22) Above all, it was highly maneuverable and could sail "[into the wind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sailing_into_the_wind "Sailing into the wind")", making it largely independent of the prevailing winds. The caravel used the [lateen sail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lateen_sail "Lateen sail"), the prevailing rig in Christian Mediterranean navigation since late antiquity.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-23) With this ship, Portuguese mariners freely explored uncharted waters around the Atlantic, from rivers and shallow waters to transoceanic voyages.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-24)

Henry sponsored voyages, collecting a 20% tax (_o quinto_) on profits, the usual practice in the Iberian states at the time. The nearby port of [Lagos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagos,_Portugal "Lagos, Portugal") provided a convenient home port for these expeditions. The voyages were made in very small ships, mostly the caravel, a light and maneuverable vessel equipped by lateen sails. Most of the voyages sent out by Henry consisted of one or two ships that navigated by following the coast, stopping at night to tie up along some shore.

During Prince Henry's time and after, the Portuguese navigators discovered and perfected the North Atlantic _[volta do mar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volta\_do\_mar "Volta do mar")_ (the "turn of the sea" or "return from the sea"): the dependable pattern of [trade winds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_winds "Trade winds") blowing largely from the east near the equator and the returning [westerlies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westerlies "Westerlies") in the mid-Atlantic. This was a major step in the history of navigation, when an understanding of [oceanic wind patterns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winds_in_the_Age_of_Sail "Winds in the Age of Sail") was crucial to Atlantic navigation, from Africa and the open ocean to Europe, and enabled the main route between the [New World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_World "New World") and Europe in the North Atlantic in future voyages of discovery. Although the lateen sail allowed [sailing upwind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_of_sail#Close-hauled "Point of sail") to some extent, it was worth even major extensions of course to have a faster and calmer [following wind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_of_sail#Running_downwind "Point of sail") for most of a journey. Portuguese mariners who sailed south and southwest towards the [Canary Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands "Canary Islands") and West Africa would afterwards sail far to the northwest—that is, away from continental Portugal, and seemingly in the wrong direction—before turning northeast near the [Azores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azores "Azores") islands and finally east to Europe in order to have largely following winds for their full journey. [Christopher Columbus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Columbus "Christopher Columbus") used this on his transatlantic voyages.

### Madeira

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Prince_Henry_the_Navigator&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Madeira")]

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cc/80._Alvise_da_Mosto%2C_o_Cadamosto_presentato_all%27_Infante_D._Enrico_di_Portogallo%2C_anno_1454.jpg/250px-80._Alvise_da_Mosto%2C_o_Cadamosto_presentato_all%27_Infante_D._Enrico_di_Portogallo%2C_anno_1454.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:80._Alvise_da_Mosto,_o_Cadamosto_presentato_all'_Infante_D._Enrico_di_Portogallo,_anno_1454.jpg)

Depiction of Prince Henry enlisting [Alvise Cadamosto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alvise_Cadamosto "Alvise Cadamosto"), who led a voyage to [Porto Santo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porto_Santo "Porto Santo"), [Madeira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madeira "Madeira"), and the [Canary Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands "Canary Islands"), before reaching the African mainland.

The first explorations followed not long after the capture of Ceuta in 1415. Henry was interested in locating the source of the [caravans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caravan_(travellers) "Caravan (travellers)") that brought gold to the city. During the reign of his father, John I, [João Gonçalves Zarco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jo%C3%A3o_Gon%C3%A7alves_Zarco "João Gonçalves Zarco") and [Tristão Vaz Teixeira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trist%C3%A3o_Vaz_Teixeira "Tristão Vaz Teixeira") were sent to explore along the African coast. Zarco, a knight in service to Prince Henry, had commanded the caravels guarding the coast of Algarve from the incursions of the [Moors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moors "Moors"). He had also been at Ceuta, along with his fellow companion [Tristão Vaz Teixeira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trist%C3%A3o_Vaz_Teixeira "Tristão Vaz Teixeira").

In 1418, Zarco and Teixeira were blown off-course by a storm while making the _volta do mar_ westward swing to return to Portugal. They found shelter at an island they named [Porto Santo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porto_Santo_Island "Porto Santo Island"). Henry directed that Porto Santo be colonized. The move to claim the [Madeiran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madeira "Madeira") islands was probably a response to [Castile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_of_Castile "Crown of Castile")'s efforts to claim the Canary Islands.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-25) In 1420, settlers then moved to the nearby island of [Madeira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madeira_Island "Madeira Island").

### The Azores

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Prince_Henry_the_Navigator&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: The Azores")]

A chart drawn by the [Catalan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalans "Catalans") cartographer, [Gabriel de Vallseca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriel_de_Vallseca "Gabriel de Vallseca") of [Mallorca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mallorca "Mallorca"), has been interpreted to indicate that the Azores were first discovered by [Diogo de Silves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diogo_de_Silves "Diogo de Silves") in 1427. In 1431, [Gonçalo Velho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gon%C3%A7alo_Velho "Gonçalo Velho") was dispatched with orders to determine the location of "islands" first identified by de Silves. Velho apparently got as far as the [Formigas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formigas "Formigas"), in the eastern archipelago, before having to return to Sagres, probably due to bad weather.

By this time the Portuguese navigators had also reached the [Sargasso Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sargasso_Sea "Sargasso Sea") (western North Atlantic region), naming it after the _[Sargassum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sargassum "Sargassum")_ seaweed growing there (_sargaço_ / _sargasso_ in Portuguese).[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-26)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-27)

### West African coast

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Prince_Henry_the_Navigator&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: West African coast")]

See also: [Portuguese raids in Senegambia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_raids_in_Senegambia "Portuguese raids in Senegambia")

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ce/Stationary_Ship_%285977153683%29.jpg/250px-Stationary_Ship_%285977153683%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Stationary_Ship_(5977153683).jpg)

Prince Henry is the central figure on the [Monument to the Discoveries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monument_to_the_Discoveries "Monument to the Discoveries") in [Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon "Lisbon").

In 1424 [Cape Bojador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Bojador "Cape Bojador") was the most southerly point known to Europeans on the west coast of Africa. For centuries, superstitious seafarers held that beyond the cape lay sea monsters and the edge of the world. However, Prince Henry was determined to know the truth. He was persistent and sent 15 expeditions over a ten-year period to pass the dreaded Cape. Each returned unsuccessful. The captains gave various excuses for having failed. Finally, in 1434 [Gil Eanes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gil_Eanes "Gil Eanes"), the commander of one of Henry's expeditions, became the first known European to pass Cape Bojador.

Using the new caravel, the expeditions then pushed onwards. [Nuno Tristão](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuno_Trist%C3%A3o "Nuno Tristão") and [Antão Gonçalves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ant%C3%A3o_Gon%C3%A7alves "Antão Gonçalves") reached [Cape Blanco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Nouadhibou "Ras Nouadhibou") in 1441. About this year, Henry he informed the Pope of his endeavours and petitioned for a concession in perpetuity to Portugal of any lands that might be discovered beyond Bojador.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:2-28) News of discovery was considered so valuable that a [Papal Bull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papal_bull "Papal bull") was immediately issued and subsequently confirmed by [Nicholas V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Nicholas_V "Pope Nicholas V") and [Sixtus IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Sixtus_IV "Pope Sixtus IV").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:2-28) Duke Peter, then acting as regent, also granted Henry the royal fifth of the produce of the expeditions, and issued a mandate that none should go on these expeditions without Henry's authorization.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:2-28)

The Portuguese sighted the [Bay of Arguin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_of_Arguin "Bay of Arguin") in 1443. This year, a company of merchants of [Lagos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagos,_Portugal "Lagos, Portugal") obtained from Prince Henry a charter for the exclusive right to trade along the African coast for a limited time, and began sending ships the following year.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:3-29) Prince Henry would later build a small fort on [Arguin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arguin "Arguin") for the accommodation of the merchants and they established a [feitoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Factory_(trading_post)#Portuguese_feitorias_(c._1445) "Factory (trading post)") there, to where they sent ships annually to sell grain, woollen cloth, linen and silver in exchange for gold dust and slaves.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-:3-29)

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/93/Jer%C3%B3nimos_Monastery_%2853825975648%29.jpg/250px-Jer%C3%B3nimos_Monastery_%2853825975648%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jer%C3%B3nimos_Monastery_(53825975648).jpg)

Prince Henry depicted in a contemporary painting.

[Dinis Dias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinis_Dias "Dinis Dias") soon came across the [Senegal River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senegal_River "Senegal River") and rounded the peninsula of [Cap-Vert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cap-Vert "Cap-Vert") in 1444. By this stage the explorers had passed the southern boundary of the desert, and from then on Henry had one of his wishes fulfilled: the Portuguese had circumvented the Muslim land-based trade routes across the western [Sahara Desert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sahara_Desert "Sahara Desert"), and slaves and gold began arriving in Portugal. This rerouting of trade devastated Algiers and Tunis, but made Portugal rich.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-30) By 1452, the influx of gold permitted the minting of Portugal's first gold _[cruzado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese\_real#Coins "Portuguese real")_ coins. A cruzado was equal to 400 reis at the time. From 1444 to 1446, as many as forty vessels sailed from [Lagos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagos,_Portugal "Lagos, Portugal") on Henry's behalf, and the first private mercantile expeditions began.

[Alvise Cadamosto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alvise_Cadamosto "Alvise Cadamosto") explored the Atlantic coast of Africa and discovered several islands of the [Cape Verde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Verde "Cape Verde") archipelago between 1453 and 1456. In his first voyage, which started on 22 March 1455, he visited the Madeira Islands and the Canary Islands. On the second voyage, in 1456, Cadamosto became the first European to reach the Cape Verde Islands. [António Noli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ant%C3%B3nio_Noli "António Noli") later claimed the credit. By 1462, the Portuguese had explored the coast of Africa as far as present-day [Sierra Leone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sierra_Leone "Sierra Leone"). Twenty-eight years later, [Bartolomeu Dias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartolomeu_Dias "Bartolomeu Dias") proved that Africa could be circumnavigated when he reached the southern tip of the continent, now known as the [Cape of Good Hope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_of_Good_Hope "Cape of Good Hope"). In 1498, [Vasco da Gama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasco_da_Gama "Vasco da Gama") became the first European sailor to reach India by sea.

## Expedition to Alcácer-Ceguer

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Prince_Henry_the_Navigator&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Expedition to Alcácer-Ceguer")]

Late in his life, Prince Henry participated in an expedition against the north-African town of [Ksar es-Seghir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ksar_es-Seghir "Ksar es-Seghir"), led by king [Afonso V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_V_of_Portugal "Afonso V of Portugal"). Ksar es-Seguir at the time served as a pirate haven for the [Marinid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marinid_dynasty "Marinid dynasty") sultan, with whom Portugal was at war.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-pessanha-31)

When the Ottomans captured Constantinople in 1453, [Pope Calixtus III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Callixtus_III "Pope Callixtus III") called for a Crusade, and the Portuguese king pledged an army.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-quintella-32) He later found to have been the only monarch to have heeded the call.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-quintella-32) Calixtus died in 6 August 1458 and Afonso decided to attack [Tangier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangier "Tangier") in Morocco instead, but was persuaded by the governor of Ceuta Sancho de Noronha to seize [Ksar es-Seghir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ksar_es-Seghir "Ksar es-Seghir") instead.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-quintella-32)

The final gathering of men and ships took place in Lagos, and the Portuguese fleet numbered 200 or 220 ships and 25,000 or 26,000 warriors, not counting sailors and supporting personnel.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-quintella-32) Henry commanded the Algarve detachment.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-quintella-32) They set sail to Alcácer-Ceguer in 12 October 1458.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-quintella-32)

## Origin of the "Navigator" nickname

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Prince_Henry_the_Navigator&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Origin of the \"Navigator\" nickname")]

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/Mosteiro_da_Batalha_-_T%C3%BAmulo_do_Henri_o_Navegador.jpg/250px-Mosteiro_da_Batalha_-_T%C3%BAmulo_do_Henri_o_Navegador.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mosteiro_da_Batalha_-_T%C3%BAmulo_do_Henri_o_Navegador.jpg)

Henry's tomb in the [Monastery of Batalha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monastery_of_Batalha "Monastery of Batalha").

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/93/Lissabon-Santa_Engracia-12-Panteao_Nacional-2011-gje_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Lissabon-Santa_Engracia-12-Panteao_Nacional-2011-gje_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lissabon-Santa_Engracia-12-Panteao_Nacional-2011-gje_(cropped).jpg)

[Cenotaph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cenotaph "Cenotaph") at the [National Pantheon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Santa_Engr%C3%A1cia "Church of Santa Engrácia") in Lisbon.

No one used the nickname "Henry the Navigator" to refer to Prince Henry during his lifetime or in the following three centuries. The term was coined by two nineteenth-century German historians, [Heinrich Schaefer](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinrich%20Sch%C3%A4fer%20(Historiker) "de:Heinrich Schäfer (Historiker)") and Gustave de Veer. It was later popularized by two British authors who included it in the titles of their biographies of the prince: Henry Major in 1868 and [Raymond Beazley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raymond_Beazley "Raymond Beazley") in 1895.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-Randles-17)

Unlike his brothers, Prince Henry was not praised for his intellectual gifts by his contemporaries. It was only later chroniclers such as [João de Barros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jo%C3%A3o_de_Barros "João de Barros") and [Damião de Góis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A3o_de_G%C3%B3is "Damião de Góis") who attributed him a scholarly character and an interest for [cosmography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmography "Cosmography"). The myth of the "[Sagres school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sagres_school "Sagres school")" allegedly founded by Prince Henry was created in the 18th century, mainly by [Samuel Purchas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Purchas "Samuel Purchas") and [Abbé Prévost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abb%C3%A9_Pr%C3%A9vost "Abbé Prévost"). In nineteenth-century Portugal, the idealized vision of Prince Henry as a putative pioneer of exploration and science reached its apogee.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-33)

## Death and legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Prince_Henry_the_Navigator&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Death and legacy")]

Henry died on the 13th of November 1460, being initially buried in the Church of Saint Mary of Lagos before being subsequently moved to the Monastery of Batalha, where his tomb remains, inscribed by his motto "Talant de bien faire".[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-34)

Henry is depicted in the [Monument of the Discoveries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monument_of_the_Discoveries "Monument of the Discoveries") located in Lisbon, featured in the front of the monument.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-35)

In 1994, the Prince Henry Society in conjunction with the Portuguese government gifted [Prince Henry the Navigator Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator_Park "Prince Henry the Navigator Park") in New Bedford, Massachusetts.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-36)

From 1996 until Portugal's adoption of [euro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euro "Euro") in 2002, he was depicted on the obverse of the largest denomination (10,000) note of the [Portuguese escudo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_escudo "Portuguese escudo").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator#cite_note-37)
